newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo '96 inflation seen under 100 pct-institute.
newsitem.headline: Yugo '96 inflation seen under 100 pct-institute.

text.p: Yugoslavia's average annual inflation for 1996 could drop to below 100 percent, a leading Yugoslav economic institute forecast on Tuesday.
After an alarming 6.6 percent rise in July over June, monthly inflation in August slowed to 2.3 percent, while the year-on-year figure was 99.2 percent.
The institute put average inflation in January-August at around 110 percent compared to the same period last year.

"We feel inflation on an annual level could drop to below 100 percent if price increases in September are under three percent, as we expect," Miroljub Labus, a prominent economist with the Belgrade Economics Institute, told reporters.
The institute's earlier forecast for 1996 inflation was 120 percent.
Labus said the relative stability in August was primarily due to a 6.6 percent seasonal drop in prices of agricultural products.
From January to August, the prices of services climbed 121 percent, industrial products 29.7 and agricultural products 19 percent.

But although retail prices were not expected to rise more than three percent in September, a higher winter rate for electricity in the fourth quarter would inevitably be accompanied by other prices hikes and could push inflation higher, Labus said.
Economists blamed the surge in July inflation on a huge rise of 10.4 percent in the price of services in that month.
"We will see what will happen from October since the heating season is approaching and the price of electricity could push the trend upwards," Bajec said.
A 4.6 percent increase in real average wages in August made up for a fall in July, and restored them to a relatively stable level of slightly over 200 German marks a month.
According to official statistics, a consumer basket of food and drinks for a family of four in August cost nearly twice as much as the average monthly wage.
But Labus said higher growth of real wages could not be sustained without a radical improvement in productivity. -- Amra Kevic, Belgrade newsroom +381 11 2224305
